topic: Why the Moon looks bigger near the horizon

sources.title: The Moon Illusion: Why Does the Moon Look So Big Sometimes?
Why Does the Moon Look Larger at the Horizon? We Asked a NASA Scientist: Episode 50
Why Does the Moon Look Bigger Near the Horizon?
Seeing Science: Solving the Mystery of the Shrinking Moon

facts.claim: Photos taken with the same camera settings show the Moon the same width near the horizon as high in the sky.
At the horizon the Moon is actually about 1.5 percent farther from you than when it is high overhead, so it is very slightly smaller in the sky.
The bigger horizon Moon is an illusion that comes from how the brain processes what the eyes see.
Scientists still do not agree on the exact cause of the Moon illusion.
A leading explanation is apparent distance: the brain judges the horizon Moon to be farther away, so it sees it as larger.
Experiments by Lloyd Kaufman and Irvin Rock around 1960 supported the apparent-distance explanation.
Held at arm's length, a fingernail covers about the same amount of Moon at the horizon as overhead.
Looking at the horizon Moon through a rolled-up paper tube makes the illusion shrink or disappear.
In a 2000 study, Lloyd and James Kaufman projected artificial moons against the real sky to test the apparent-distance explanation.
